first_impression.reaction: My assistant found this while building our master timeline. The first screen is calm and serious about lead times, no gushing, no prices. But it's a checklist for a couple doing it themselves. Her summary: 'Solid month-by-month list, good on passports and overseas paperwork, written for a standard wedding, nothing on large guest numbers, security or privacy.' I read the takeaways, skimmed the destination tracks and read the close.

journey.quote: A year sounds like a long time until you count the things that cannot be rushed: a venue on your date, a gown made to measure, a passport renewal, legal papers for marrying overseas.
journey.reaction: Understated and practical. A good first line.

journey.section: How does a 12 month checklist change for a destination wedding?
journey.quote: Overseas, the paperwork, the passports and your guests' travel all have lead times you cannot shorten by paying more or working late.
journey.reaction: True, and refreshingly honest. Money doesn't fix a consulate. This sounds like people who've done it.

journey.section: 12 months out: what to do first
journey.quote: Agree what you will spend and who is contributing, in writing between the two of you, before any venue conversation.
journey.reaction: Written for a couple splitting costs. For us the family office sets this. It tells me who the page is really for.

journey.section: 12 months out: what to do first
journey.quote: Decide whether you want a planner, and bring them in now so they can shape the venue choice rather than inherit it.
journey.reaction: Correct. We would have a planner before the venue. Good advice.

journey.section: 10 to 11 months out: book the people who shape the day
journey.quote: Hold a block of rooms for guests close to the venue, with a release date agreed in writing.
journey.reaction: A room block. For 300 guests we'd want the whole property, closed to the public. Nothing here on exclusive use.

journey.section: 10 to 11 months out: book the people who shape the day
journey.quote: Set up a wedding website or RSVP page where guests can find travel details as they firm up.
journey.reaction: A public wedding website is the last thing we'd do. No mention of keeping details private or password protected.

journey.section: 8 to 9 months out: attire, accommodation and the celebrant
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor is the one person who plans with you from start to finish, works in your time zone and agrees the fee in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: One contact suits me, fewer people means fewer leaks. Fee in writing is fine. But nothing says they've handled a wedding my size.

journey.section: 6 to 7 months out: rings, stationery and the details
journey.quote: Start a ceremony plan with your celebrant: order of service, music, readings and any family customs.
journey.reaction: At least family customs are acknowledged. One phrase, but it's there and it doesn't stereotype.

journey.quote: Collect the small items: guest book, signage, place cards, favours.
journey.reaction: This is someone else's job in my world. The page reads as if I'm packing boxes myself.

journey.section: Your 12 month wedding checklist at a glance
journey.quote: For a printable version alongside real weddings and destination ideas, sign up for the [Wedded Wonderland magazine](https://weddedwonderland.com/magazine?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=12-month-wedding-checklist&utm_content=magnet).
journey.reaction: A magazine sign-up for a printable list. Mass-market. My assistant wouldn't hand over an email for this.

unanswered_questions: Have you planned weddings for 200 to 400 guests with VIP logistics, and can you show me one discreetly? (deferred business detail)
Can you arrange exclusive use of a whole property, closed to the public for several days? (deferred business detail)
How do you work with a private security team alongside the venue's? (deferred business detail)
How do you protect privacy: NDAs for suppliers, no phones, no social posting, private guest information instead of a public website? (deferred business detail)
Do you arrange private transfers and aviation for guests, and handle guests' passports and visas at scale? (deferred business detail)
Can you work through a family office and quote outside AUD? (deferred business detail)

turn_offs_found.quote: Pack an emergency kit, and plan a meal for your suppliers if the venue does not.
turn_offs_found.why: Over-explaining for a self-planned wedding. At my level a production team handles this, and seeing it listed for me makes the brand feel like it serves standard clients.

turn_offs_found.quote: Rest, eat well and keep the day before light.
turn_offs_found.why: Eager, hand-holding tone. I don't need to be told to eat; it reads as generic advice for everyone.

turn_offs_found.quote: Set an RSVP date that leaves you time to chase late replies before final numbers are due.
turn_offs_found.why: Basic housekeeping written to the couple. It signals that I'd be doing the chasing, which is exactly the standard-client experience I want to avoid.

would_share_with: My assistant would forward the destination track (passports, CNI, legalisation timings) to our planner and the family office. Nobody else.

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready, [talk to Wedded Concierge](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=12-month-wedding-checklist&utm_content=closing) about your date and destination.
cta_reaction.why: Calm and not pushy, which I respect. But I don't enquire through a blog link, and nothing here proves scale, exclusive use or discretion. I'd want a private introduction.

top_3_changes: Add one line in the destination track for large weddings: exclusive use of the property instead of a room block, private transfers, and coordinating private security with the venue's, phrased as things to ask, without brand claims that need sourcing.
Add a privacy note next to the wedding website advice: keep guest details private or password protected and ask suppliers about confidentiality and social posting.
Trim the hand-holding lines ('Rest, eat well and keep the day before light.', the emergency kit) or frame them as tasks to delegate, so the page reads less like a DIY list.

checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
Journey types limited to gained_trust, lost_trust, confused, bored, excited, objection
Stayed in character as Layla (uhnw): assistant-first skim, judged from the first screen, looked for scale, discretion and cultural awareness, put off by over-explaining and standard-client content
No invented brand facts; scale proof, exclusive use, security, privacy, transfers and currency listed in unanswered_questions as deferred
VERIFY markers and HTML comments (fact tags, image slots) ignored

open_questions.question: A generic 12 month checklist is structurally low relevance for Layla; the low enquiry score mostly reflects the topic. The public wedding website and room block advice are the points that most signal 'standard client' to her and could be balanced with one privacy and exclusive-use line.

The persona is provisional and not calibrated with the CRM, so confidence is 0.75.
